lines.text: Kings and reformers, an empire's capital, occupation and a revolution without bloodshed. This is the story of the Czech lands, from Great Moravia to today.
In the eight hundreds Great Moravia rose, the first great Slavic state of Central Europe, where the missionaries Cyril and Methodius preached.
From here grew the Czech lands, heirs to the kingdom of Bohemia, though the Czech Republic itself would only be born in 1993.
On the river Vltava, Prague took shape, a city that would come to be known for its hundred spires.
Above it rose Prague Castle, the largest old castle complex in the world, home of kings and now of presidents.
In 1198 Bohemia became a kingdom, its rulers among the electors who chose the Holy Roman Emperor.
In 1348 King Charles the Fourth founded a university in Prague, the first in Central Europe.
A few years later he began the great stone bridge across the Vltava that still bears his name.
Jan Hus, a preacher who taught at the university, called for reform of the church. In 1415 he was burned at the stake.
In 1410 the astronomical clock was set on the Old Town Hall. It is the oldest of its kind still working.
In 1419 angry Hussites threw city officials from a window, and two centuries later a second such fall would set off the Thirty Years' War.
In 1620 the Bohemian rebels were crushed at White Mountain, and the Czech lands lost their independence for three centuries.
In 1805, on Moravian fields near Austerlitz, Napoleon won his greatest victory over Russia and Austria.
In a monastery garden in Brno, the friar Gregor Mendel bred thousands of pea plants and found the laws of heredity.
Antonin Dvorak filled his music with the dance rhythms of Bohemia, and in America wrote his New World Symphony.
Tomas Masaryk, a philosopher, would found Czechoslovakia and become its first president.
Franz Kafka, a Prague insurance clerk who wrote in German, imagined people trapped by faceless systems. Most of his work appeared after his death.
In 1895 the firm that became Skoda Auto was founded in Mlada Boleslav, and it still builds cars there.
In 1918, as Austria-Hungary collapsed, Czechs and Slovaks made a state of their own: Czechoslovakia.
Emil Zatopek, the Czech Locomotive, would win the five, the ten thousand metres and the marathon at the 1952 Olympics.
Vaclav Havel, a playwright, would be jailed as a dissident, and then lead his country to freedom as its president.
In 1938, at Munich, Britain and France let Hitler take the Sudetenland. The Czechs were not even at the table.
Jan Palach was born the year the communists took power. As a student he would give his life in protest.
Andrej Babis, a billionaire businessman, would later become prime minister, and again after the election of 2025.
In 1968 Alexander Dubcek promised socialism with a human face. In August, Warsaw Pact tanks rolled in and ended the Prague Spring.
In November 1989 students marched, crowds filled the squares, and within weeks communist rule was over. Havel became president.
Then, just as peacefully, Czechs and Slovaks parted. On the first day of 1993 the Czech Republic stood on its own.
From the kings of Bohemia to the Velvet Revolution, Prague's hundred spires have watched it all.
